definition: Antecedent means something that came before and led toward what followed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word antecedent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know antecedent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The judge traced the privacy ruling to its eighteenth-century antecedent, a case about letters opened by a village postmaster.
An influence is milder than an antecedent — a designer may absorb a hundred influences, but an antecedent stands in the direct line that led to the work.
A prototype goes further than an antecedent: it is an early working version of the thing itself, while an antecedent only came before and opened the way.

A forerunner comes before and points the way — the emphasis is the pointing, a preview of the direction things will take. An antecedent makes the firmer historical claim: it stands in the direct line of descent that led to what followed, whether or not it ever looked ahead.

A forebear is an ancestor, almost always a person in a family line — your great-grandmother, not her recipes. An antecedent traces the same backward line through things and ideas: rulings, inventions, customs. Keep forebear for people; use antecedent for the earlier thing an idea grew from.

Antecedent means something that came before and led toward what followed.
Food historians point to the Roman libum — a small cheesecake baked over bay leaves and offered on household birthdays — as an antecedent of the modern birthday cake.
No unbroken recipe connects the two, and nobody in Rome iced anything.
What travelled was the idea: mark the day a person was born with something sweet, made for them alone.
Antecedent fits because the libum came before and led toward the birthday cake without being an early version of it.
The word claims a line of descent, not identity — an antecedent opens the path that later things walk down, which is a more careful claim than calling it the first birthday cake.
Antecedent is the scholar's word for what came before and fed into what followed — rulings, inventions, customs, styles.

(Grammar borrows it too: the noun a pronoun points back to is called its antecedent.) Note the direction against another word in this unit: an antecedent is found by looking backward from a thing to what led to it, while a harbinger looks forward, announcing what has not yet arrived.

Every skyscraper textbook opens with Chicago in the 1880s, but the tall building did not spring from nowhere.
Its true antecedent stood in the English Midlands a century earlier: the iron-framed flax mill, whose metal skeleton carried the floors so the walls no longer had to.
The mill was squat and windowless, and nobody called it beautiful.
Yet every load-bearing trick the Chicago engineers used descends from that frame.
Architectural historians are careful with the claim.
Plenty of buildings before 1880 were merely tall, and plenty of engineers had clever ideas that led nowhere.
The mill is different: documents show the Chicago firms studying its drawings, so the line of descent is direct, not a matter of family resemblance.
